idiom_name: struct/class conforming to the expected protocol and forwarding to the adaptee
implementation_notes: Swift expresses the adapter as a type that conforms to the protocol the caller expects and forwards each requirement to the wrapped value; the wrapper is hand-written, but the compiler checks the conformance, and a single-requirement protocol can be satisfied by a closure or function value instead. For protocols with associated types, where the protocol cannot be used as a standalone type, the standard library's Any-prefixed erasers (AnySequence, AnyIterator, AnyCollection) are the same idea shipped: each forwards its operations to a boxed base value and hides its concrete type. Use a protocol-conforming wrapper for behavioural adaptation and a type eraser when the problem is an existential such as 'any Sequence of Int'.
pitfalls: A struct adapter copies: sharing a reference-type adaptee between copies is usually intended, but mutating wrapper methods then need `mutating` and a clear sense of which copy owns the state.
Retain cycles: a class adapter that stores the adaptee while the adaptee stores or captures the adapter leaks without [weak self].
Conformances declared in extensions in other files hide where the adapter lives; keep the conformance next to the wrapper unless the protocol requires otherwise.
A closure-based single-requirement adapter captures its context and can retain it; escaping closures in long-lived adapters are a common leak source.

variants.name: Closure-boxed type eraser
variants.implementation_notes: When the target protocol has associated types, it cannot be used as an existential, so the adapter becomes a box: keep the concrete adaptee in a private class (or a generic subclass) and store the operations to expose as closures, then conform the box to the protocol. This is the technique behind AnySequence/AnyIterator, which forward to an arbitrary base value. Choose it when the caller needs 'any Sequence of Int' rather than a behavioural wrapper; prefer the plain protocol-conforming wrapper when no existential is required.
variants.idiom_name: type-erased wrapper storing the base's operations as closures (AnySequence pattern)
pitfalls: The box hides the concrete type permanently - the base value cannot be recovered, so do not erase types you will later need to inspect.
Storing one closure per forwarded requirement bloats the wrapper; for large protocols use the standard library's single-box subclass technique or avoid erasure altogether.
The boxed base is captured by the closures, so a class with mutating state is shared after erasure - and the standard library marks AnySequence as not Sendable for exactly this reason.
